source_text: Hoc enim nihil, de quo facta sunt omnia, affirmas causam fuisse peccati. Tantum igitur facit apud te nihili huius potentia, quantum apud Manichaeum principis tenebrarum. Ambo ergo dicitis etiam primi mali necessitatem fuisse; sed dat ille soliditatem vel malam; tu inanitatem, aeque tamen malam: ille ergo dicit violentam substantiam; tu violentum aeque, sed nihilum. Vide ergo syllogismi tui finem: nihilum nempe, cum necdum quidquam esset creatum, aeternae erat inanitatis indicium; sed hoc ipsum nihilum, id est, inanitas, orientibus est finita creaturis; desivit enim nihil esse, cum coepit aliquid esse. Ipsum ergo nihilum etiam cum erat, non erat; quoniam tunc intellegitur fuisse, cum necdum aliquid erat. Postea vero quam factae res sunt, hoc inanitatis indicium, id est, nihilum, sicut substantiam numquam habuerat, ita etiam vocabulum suum perdidit; factumque est, ut quod in re numquam extiterat, etiam ipsum nomen amitteret. Huius ergo tu violentia malum et in angelo et in homine commentaris exortum; quo quid furiosius dici potest?
pass_a_gloss: For this nothing, from which all things were made, you affirm was the cause of sin. So much therefore does the power of this nothing do with you, as with Manichaeus that of the prince of darkness. Both therefore say there was a necessity even of the first evil; but he gives a solidity even evil; you an emptiness, equally nevertheless evil: he therefore says a violent substance; you equally violent, but nothing. See therefore the end of your syllogism: nothing indeed, when not yet anything had been created, was a sign of eternal emptiness; but this nothing itself, that is emptiness, was finished by arising creatures; for it ceased to be nothing, when something began to be. That nothing itself therefore even when it was, was not; because it is then understood to have been, when not yet something was. But after things were made, this sign of emptiness, that is nothing, as it had never had substance, so it also lost its own word; and it was done that what had never existed in the thing even lost the name itself. By the violence of this therefore you invent evil arisen both in an angel and in a human; than which what more furious can be said?

pass_b_english: For you affirm that this nothing, from which all things were made, was sin’s cause. The power of this nothing therefore accomplishes as much for you as the prince of darkness does for Mani. Both of you say that even the first evil arose by necessity. But he supplies something solid, although evil; you supply emptiness, equally evil. He therefore says there is a violent substance; you say there is something equally violent, but nothing. See, then, the conclusion of your syllogism. When nothing had yet been created, ‘nothing’ indicated eternal emptiness. But this very nothing—that is, emptiness—was brought to an end when creatures arose: it ceased to be nothing when something began to be. Thus even when this nothing was, it was not, since it is understood to have been only when nothing yet existed. After things were made, this indication of emptiness—nothing—lost even its name, just as it had never possessed substance. Thus what had never existed in reality lost even its name. You invent the claim that by its violence evil arose in both angel and human being. What could be more insane?
